newsitem.title: Yemen: Yemen ruling party advances in general election.
newsitem.headline: Yemen ruling party advances in general election.

text.p: Yemen's ruling General Peoples Congress (GPC) on Tuesday made strong gains in initial general election results while its Islamist junior coalition partner slipped in the country's first poll since a 1994 civil war.
Saeed al-Hekaimi, spokesman for the Supreme Elections Committee, told a news conference that as of 4.00 p.m. (1300 GMT) the GPC had swept two-thirds of the 135 constituencies counted.
The ruling party had so far won 93 seats in the 301-seat parliament while its Islah Party coalition partner won 16.
Independents took 24 seats and other parties won two in Sunday's elections.
In the crucial race in the capital Sanaa, 13 out of 18 constituencies went to the GPC.
The GPC had so far won three constituencies out of a total of 11 in the southern port city of Aden, one went to Islah and two to independents.
Two women were among the winners in Aden.
Western diplomats have said the GPC is expected to win a big majority in this year's race, seen as a key test of Yemen's fledgling democracy. Full results are expected by Thursday.
The diplomats describe Yemen's parliament as a pressure group and say power ultimately lies with President Ali Abdullah Saleh, appointed ministers and military and security forces loyal to his GPC.
The elections and pre-election period have been marred by several violent attacks which have claimed more than 10 lives.

In the most recent incident, Hekaimi said two people were killed on Monday when a Yemeni citizen hurled a hand-grenade at security officers in the governorate of Taiz, 260 km (160 miles) south of the capital Sanaa.

"What happened unfortunately is that a citizen threw a hand-grenade at a security unit. There were two martyrs," he said. "Investigations are underway on the matter. This is not an election dispute or an election crime. It's a criminal act."

In united Yemen's first elections in 1993, the GPC won 123 seats in parliament followed by Islah with 62 and the Yemen Socialist Party (YSP), 56. Independents won 47 seats while the rest went to Baathist and Nasserite parties.
"The GPC will win. More independents could be in and the Islah could lose some seats," said one Western diplomat. "The Islah portfolio has many political minefields."

He was referring to Islah ministers occupying government portfolios such as electricity and water and health which are crucial to the average citizen and sensitive in Yemen, one of the Arab world's poorest countries.
The GPC holds key ministries such as defence, finance, interior and foreign affairs.
"The Islah are in portfolios which are very hard to deliver on at a time of economic hardship," a Yemeni analyst said.
Parliamentary speaker Sheikh Abdullah bin Hussein al-Ahmar of the Islah has accused the GPC of hampering vote counting by moving some ballot boxes to military camps, a charge denied by the GPC.
Diplomats said tension had been rising between the GPC and Islah in the run-up to the poll. A man was killed when clashes broke out between supporters of the two parties on April 20.

The main opposition YSP, some of whose leaders launched the separatist bid that triggered the 1994 civil war, and three other parties boycotted the polls due to alleged irregularities. The government denies the accusations.
